summary: This memo specifies a Telnet option for passing environment information, such as variable settings, from a client to a server. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1408 defines a Telnet option for passing environment settings between a client and a server. The receiving host can use, ignore or handle each setting in a way that fits its own system.

questions: what is the telnet environment option
how does telnet send environment variables
subtitle: A Telnet option for requesting and exchanging environment variables.

tldr.problem: A remote Telnet host may need startup settings from the client, but a separate option for every setting would require many protocol additions.
tldr.mechanism: The ENVIRON option lets one side request named variables with SEND and the other return them with IS. INFO carries later changes, and variable markers distinguish well-known names from user-defined ones.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1408 is marked Historic and the batch metadata says RFC 1571 updated it.

today: RFC 1408 is marked Historic, and the batch metadata lists RFC 1571 as updating it. This memo describes the earlier ENVIRON specification.

sections.title: Why Exchange Environment Information
sections.content:
Operating systems may keep startup information in environment variables. A client can send this information to a remote host when a Telnet connection is established. A generic option avoids defining a separate Telnet option whenever a new kind of information is needed.

The option is disabled by default: WONT ENVIRON and DONT ENVIRON mean that the sides will not exchange environment information unless they negotiate otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: The option gives Telnet one way to carry different startup settings. Both computers must agree to use it before they exchange those settings.

sections.title: Negotiation, Requests and Replies
sections.content:
The option code is 36. WILL ENVIRON says a sender is willing to send variables; DO ENVIRON says a sender is willing to receive them. The receiver side may request variables with SEND, and the sender side replies with IS.

A request can name particular variables or ask for the default set. The reply returns requested entries in the same order. A missing value means a variable is undefined; a value marker followed immediately by another marker means it is defined but empty. INFO reports changes after initial exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: One side asks for settings, and the side that agreed to send them replies with names and values. A separate message can report changes later.

sections.title: Variable Types and Well-Known Names
sections.content:
VAR marks a well-known variable and USERVAR marks a user-defined variable. The memo names USER, JOB, ACCT, PRINTER, SYSTEMTYPE and DISPLAY. Their value formats may depend on the remote system; the printer format is left undefined.

Users can supply other variable names as USERVAR entries. The RFC notes that software should treat received values cautiously and that the outcome of a name collision between the two types depends on the implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: Some settings have names defined by the protocol, such as USER and DISPLAY. USERVAR lets a user send other names, but the server decides what it will accept.

sections.title: Using the Values
sections.content:
The DO and WILL exchange grants permission for later requests. The side that sent DO may request variables; the side that sent WILL may send them. Although the option can be used at any time, the RFC expects most exchanges to happen when the connection starts.

The receiving host does not have to store every value in its environment. It may ignore a variable it does not understand or one already learned more accurately through another option. An empty IS response is valid when no variables are defined.
sections.plainLanguage: The server chooses how to use the settings it receives. It may ignore a setting that it does not need or already knows from another source.

sections.title: Security Concerns
sections.content:
The RFC asks implementers to examine how environment settings interact with login and authentication. They should decide which variables are safe to set before the user has logged in.

The memo warns that allowing a variable to change could let an intruder bypass or compromise the login or authentication program.
sections.plainLanguage: A setting received before login could affect the login process itself. Implementers need to check which settings are safe to accept at that point.
